title: Tsunami_Kaiten_Incident_Response_Scenario_0f3
description: Investigate and respond to a Tsunami/Kaiten malware incident on the target system.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
The Tsunami/Kaiten malware is a Unix Trojan known as Tsunami/Kaiten.c, which operates as an IRC/Bot with flooder and backdoor capabilities. It exploits web admin panel abuse via HTTP access to gain root privilege through crontab UID manipulation. The malware deletes source traces and logs, runs and hides its service using a fake bash process, and communicates via IRC ports.

Your task is to investigate and respond to this incident on the target system. This scenario will teach you how to identify and analyze suspicious services, determine persistence mechanisms, and locate malicious executables using systemd commands.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
You have SSH access to the target system with the following credentials:
- Hostname: target
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano
levels.local_content: Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario. Enter the word `start` to proceed to the next level.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Services
levels.content:
Investigate the target system for any unauthorized or suspicious services running.

Question: What is the name of the suspicious service you identified?
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, check the systemd services using the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` and look for any unusual or unfamiliar services. The suspicious service is a systemd service named `tsunami-kaiten.service`. The flag type is the service name.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Start by understanding how systemd manages services on the system. Use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for services that might not belong to standard system operations. Pay attention to any services with unusual names or descriptions. Use the command `systemctl status <service-name>` to check the status of a specific service.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The suspicious service is a systemd service named `tsunami-kaiten.service`. The flag type is the service name.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content:
Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot.

Question: What is the persistence mechanism used by the suspicious service?
levels.solution: Examine the systemd unit files and timers using the command `systemctl list-timers` to understand how the service is scheduled to run. The persistence mechanism is a systemd timer named `tsunami-kaiten.timer`. The flag type is the timer name.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Understand how systemd timers can be used to schedule services. Use the command `systemctl list-timers` to list all timers.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for timers that might be associated with the suspicious service. Pay attention to any timers with unusual names or descriptions. Use the command `systemctl status <timer-name>` to check the status of a specific timer.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The persistence mechanism is a systemd timer named `tsunami-kaiten.timer`. The flag type is the timer name.

levels.title: Locate Executable or File
levels.content:
Locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious activity.

Question: What is the path to the executable or file associated with the suspicious service?
levels.solution: Investigate the service unit files using the command `systemctl cat tsunami-kaiten.service` to find the path to the executable or file. The path to the executable is a shell script located at `/usr/local/bin/tsunami-kaiten.sh`. The flag type is the file path.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Understand how systemd services reference their executable files. Use the command `systemctl cat tsunami-kaiten.service` to view the service unit file.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for the executable path in the service unit file. Pay attention to the `ExecStart` line in the unit file. Use the command `cat /usr/local/bin/tsunami-kaiten.sh` to inspect the script.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The path to the executable is a shell script located at `/usr/local/bin/tsunami-kaiten.sh`. The flag type is the file path.
